Chapter 1: Introduction. Before we write a single YAML file, we need a clear picture of what CI/CD is, which problem it solves, and why machine learning makes it more interesting than in ordinary software.

After this level you can:

  • Explain CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment in your own words, and say how they differ.
  • Describe what a pipeline is and why it fails fast.
  • Name the three things that change in an ML system (code, data, configuration) and why evaluation becomes a quality gate.
  • Know which tool in this book does what, and in which level you will meet it.

Imagine two small ML teams in Berlin. Both have four engineers, both serve a credit-risk model behind an HTTP API, and both deploy on a Friday.

Team A has no CI/CD. Lena finishes a feature on Thursday: a new input field age. Her tests pass on her laptop, so she copies the model file to the server, restarts the service and goes home. On Friday morning Jonas merges his own change, which was written against last week's code. He never ran Lena's tests, and Lena never ran his. The service starts, but every request with age crashes with a KeyError. Nobody notices until a customer calls. Rolling back means finding the "old" model file somewhere on a laptop. The team loses a day, and next time everyone is afraid to deploy, so they deploy less often, so each deployment contains more changes, so each one is riskier. This vicious circle is the normal state of teams without automation.

Team B has CI/CD. Lena opens a pull request. Within four minutes a robot (the CI server) installs the project from scratch on a clean machine, runs the linters, the unit tests and a small training run, and checks that the model's accuracy has not dropped. A red cross appears next to Jonas's PR, because it conflicts with Lena's change. He updates his branch and the cross turns green. After a review, the merge to main automatically builds a Docker image, deploys it to a staging environment, runs a smoke test, and waits for one click to go to production. When something does go wrong, a "rollback" button redeploys the previous image in two minutes.
Team B is not smarter than team A. It has simply moved the boring, error-prone steps from human memory into code that runs the same way every time. That code is what this book teaches you to write.

Concept: Continuous Integration (CI)

Every change is merged into the shared main branch often (at least daily) and every merge is automatically built and tested. The goal is to find integration problems minutes after they are created, while the author still remembers the code. German: kontinuierliche Integration.

Concept: Continuous Delivery (CD)

Every change that passes CI is automatically turned into a release candidate (for us: a Docker image) and deployed to a test environment. Going to production is a business decision, taken with one click. German: kontinuierliche Bereitstellung (Bereitstellung = deployment).

Concept: Continuous Deployment

Like continuous delivery, but without the click: every green change goes to production automatically. This needs very good tests and monitoring. Many teams, and most ML teams, stop at continuous delivery with a manual approval for production.

A pipeline is the automated sequence of stages that a change travels through (Figure 1). Each stage only runs if the previous one succeeded; that is called failing fast. A failing linter stops the pipeline after 20 seconds instead of after a 15-minute training run. A pipeline is described as code (YAML files in the repository), so it is versioned, reviewed and reproducible, exactly like the application itself.

cards.html:
TimeWhat runsIf it fails here, it means…
10:48Pipeline pauses: "Review deployments".–
11:15Lead approves → production deploy + smoke test.Rare by now; if so, roll back to the previous SHA in two minutes.

Notice the shape: the earliest checks are the cheapest and catch the most common mistakes; each later stage catches a class of problem the earlier ones cannot see. A pipeline is a funnel of increasingly expensive, increasingly realistic tests. When you design one, ask of every stage: what kind of mistake does this catch that nothing before it can? If the answer is "nothing", delete the stage.

What if… the tests pass on Lena's laptop but fail in CI?

What happens: The PR shows a red cross although "it works for me".

Why: CI starts from a clean machine with only what is committed. The usual culprits: a file that is in .gitignore (data, a model, a .env), a package installed by hand but missing from uv.lock, an absolute path like /Users/lena/data.csv, a different time zone, or test order (one test relies on state another test left behind).

cards.sub: Worked example: one change, minute by minute
cards.html:
What you do: Treat this as a success of CI: it found an assumption that would also have broken production. Reproduce it with a fresh clone (git clone <url> /tmp/x, then uv sync --locked && uv run pytest inside it). Level 1 shows how to read the log.

What if… two PRs are both green, but main is red after merging both?

What happens: Lena's PR renames a function; Jonas's PR adds a new call to the old name. Each PR was tested against the main it started from. Git merges both without a conflict, because they touched different files. The combination is broken.

Why: CI tested each change alone, not the combination. This is a semantic conflict; Chapter 2 reproduces one.

cards.sub: Worked example: one change, minute by minute
cards.html: What you do: Require branches to be up to date before merging (Level 2), or use a merge queue, which tests the exact combination before it lands. And always run CI on main after every merge, so the breakage is found within minutes, not by a customer.

A few more words that you will hear daily:

TermMeaning
WorkflowGitHub's name for a pipeline definition: one YAML file in .github/workflows/.
Job / stepA workflow contains jobs (each runs on its own fresh virtual machine); a job contains steps (single commands).
RunnerThe machine that executes a job. GitHub provides hosted Linux, Windows and macOS runners.
ArtefactA file produced by a pipeline and kept afterwards: a coverage report, a trained model, a Docker image.
EnvironmentA place where the application runs: dev, staging (production-like, for testing), production (real users).
Quality gateA check that must pass for the pipeline to continue: tests, coverage threshold, model accuracy.
RollbackReturning production to the previous working version.

In classic software, the behaviour of a system is determined by its code. If the code does not change, the behaviour does not change. In machine learning, behaviour is determined by code, data and configuration together (Figure 2). Retraining with the same code on new data gives you a different model. The same data with a different random seed gives a slightly different model. This has consequences for CI/CD:

1. Version more than code. You must be able to say which data snapshot and which hyper-parameters produced the model in production. Tools: Git for code, DVC or data snapshots for data, MLflow for runs and models.
  2. Evaluation is a test. A model can be "correct code" and still be bad. So the pipeline trains (on a sample, to stay fast), measures metrics and fails the build if they drop. We call this an accuracy gate (Level 4).
  3. Tests are statistical, not exact. You do not assert an exact prediction such as 0.7312; you assert properties: probabilities between 0 and 1, determinism with a fixed seed, metric above a floor.

1. Data can break things without any commit. A new upstream column format breaks training. Data validation tests (a "data contract") catch this, and scheduled pipelines run them even when nobody pushes.
  2. LLM systems need evaluation with cost control. A RAG service is evaluated against a golden set of questions. Calls to an LLM cost money, so CI must decide when to run the expensive checks.

What if… nobody changes the code, but the model gets worse?

What happens: Three months after deployment, the credit model approves more bad loans. No commit was made; every pipeline run was green.

Why: The world changed, not the code: inflation shifted credit_amount, a new loan purpose appeared, a partner bank sends different applicants. This is data drift (the inputs change) or concept drift (the relation between inputs and outcome changes). A push-triggered pipeline cannot see it, because nothing was pushed.

What you do: Add time-triggered pipelines: nightly data validation against the newest data, a weekly retraining that must beat the current champion (Level 4), and monitoring of the live prediction distribution. In ML, "nothing changed in Git" never means "nothing changed".

What if… the new model is better on average but worse for one group?

What happens: ROC-AUC goes up from 0.786 to 0.792, the gate passes, but for applicants under 25 the model got clearly worse.

Why: One average metric hides subgroups. In credit-api the gap is real: on the test set, AUC is 0.80 for applicants aged 25 and over but only 0.74 for the 48 applicants under 25 (Level 4 measures this).

What you do: Make the gate check slices that matter for your business and for fairness, not only the overall number. For a credit model in the EU this is not optional: the AI Act classes credit scoring as high-risk.

Interview tip

"In ML, a green unit-test suite is necessary but not sufficient. I treat model evaluation as a quality gate in CI: the build fails if the new model is worse than the one in production, and data validation runs before training so we fail on bad data, not on a bad model."

Figure 3 shows where you are going. Each level builds on the previous one and ends with a checkpoint. You use one running example, a credit-risk API called credit-api, from Level 1 to the first half of Level 4; then a second example, rag-api, for LLM evaluation. Two chapters sit beside the levels: Operate it (Chapter 7: logs, SLOs, incidents, cost and compliance after deployment) and The senior toolkit (Chapter 9: system design, interview answers and turning the projects into a portfolio).

Watch out: AWS costs money

Levels 1, 2 and 4 are free if your repository is public (GitHub Actions minutes are free for public repositories). Level 3 creates AWS resources that cost roughly 1 to 2 US dollars per day while they run. Chapter 5 sets up budget alarms first and ends with a cleanup script. Run it at the end of each session.
